newsitem.title: USA: Opposition mounts to Florida Medfly spraying.
newsitem.headline: Opposition mounts to Florida Medfly spraying.

text.p: Opponents of aerial pesticide spraying against the Mediterranean fruit fly complained on Wednesday that poison was wafting into major waterways in west-central Florida.
As a multimillion dollar effort to eradicate the agricultural pest continued into its sixth week, concerns mounted about the possible environmental and health dangers from the programme.

U.S. and state agriculture officials say malathion, the pesticide bait being used to kill the bugs, is safe. But the programme is under growing fire from a community group called Citizens for Responsible Application of Malathion (CRAM).

"The Agriculture Department is spraying the pesticide within 200 meters of our major waterways and in some instances has sprayed the poison into our major waterways," Bonnie Burns of CRAM said at a Hillsborough County commission hearing Wednesday.
The commission will meet on the issue again next week.
CRAM, joined by Hillsborough County Commissioner Joe Chillura, wants the spraying replaced with alternative eradication methods such as the release of sterile fruit flies.
The sterile flies, which mate with wild flies and end the reproduction cycle, have been used to combat the Medfly in other areas.

Malathion spraying by DC-3 aircraft and helicopters began in late May shortly after the first flies were discovered in Hillsborough County. Mediterranean fruit flies can harm more than 200 types of fruit and vegetables and are considered a major threat to Florida's $8 billion citrus industry.
The area being sprayed now covers more than 400 square miles including parts of downtown Tampa and residential areas.
A few flies also have been found in nearby Polk County, the most productive citrus-growing region in the state.
Residents were warned to stay indoors when spray planes are overhead and to wash cars immediately to prevent damage.

"The public cannot understand how malathion is not harmful when it is capable of damaging the paint on your car from just one overfly if the car is not washed in a short period of time," Chillura said in a statement last week.

The Environmental Protection Agency banned spraying within 200 yards or meters of lakes and rivers. High levels of malathion have been found in some local bodies of water but later tests found the levels had returned to normal.
Spraying was expected to continue at least through the end of July before the sterile flies are released.
